audioScript:
Good morning, Midya. It's Monday, June twenty-ninth, twenty twenty-six. Here's what matters today — and there's a lot that connects directly to your consulting pivot and life in BC right now.

Let's start with AI, because two stories landed this morning that together paint a picture of where the technology is headed — and where the battles are about to be fought.

First, the most consequential AI governance story in months: the pro-AI coalition in Washington is fracturing. David Sacks — Trump's former AI and crypto czar — issued a public warning this weekend that restricting American companies' access to export their most advanced AI models risks undermining the entire US strategy to out-compete China. This is significant. A year ago, Trump declared a global AI race and positioned America as the undisputed leader. Now, inside the administration, national-security hawks are pushing for export controls that would limit what AI models can be shared internationally — and the Silicon Valley faction is pushing back hard and publicly. The fight is happening in real time, in the open, and it has direct implications for Canada. Canadian AI policy, federal research funding, and the AI partnerships that Canadian universities are building with US firms are all downstream of however Washington resolves this. If you're advising a Canadian university on AI strategy — and you should be — this is the geopolitical headwind to name in your presentations. The risk isn't that AI slows down. The risk is that the global infrastructure for AI collaboration gets carved into blocs, and Canada has to decide which side of that fence it's standing on.

The second AI story is more immediately useful for your practice: agentic AI was the dominant theme at Cannes Lions 2026, which wrapped last week. Nvidia, Yahoo, Palantir, Pinterest, and Fox all unveiled what can only be described as foundational infrastructure — interconnected AI agents that talk to each other and execute marketing tasks that were previously done by humans. Campaign planning, creative testing, media buying optimization, audience segmentation — these are now agentic workflows, not human workflows. The message from Cannes is that agentic capability is no longer a future promise; it's the baseline expectation. If you're walking into a Canadian university marketing department or a corporate CMO conversation, and you're not speaking fluently about agentic AI in marketing, you're already behind the curve. The good news is that most of your potential clients aren't there yet either — which is precisely where a consultant with your background should be positioning. The window to be the person who translates agentic AI into practical institutional strategy is open right now, but it won't stay open for long.

Also worth a note: Canada's UN ambassador made news this morning positioning Ottawa as a champion for safe and equitable AI adoption at the United Nations. This is diplomatic signalling more than policy action, but it matters for your context. It tells you that the Canadian federal government wants to be seen as the reasonable middle path between American permissiveness and European restriction. That's a brand position — and it creates space for Canadian institutions to lean into responsible AI adoption as a competitive differentiator.

Staying close to the marketing thread, because this morning had some genuinely useful content for your practice.

Omnicom CEO John Wren sat down for a candid interview and revealed what comes next for the agency behemoth after its IPG merger. He's selling off businesses that don't fit the AI-driven future — he specifically called out things like mud flap manufacturers and cheese samplers, which is his way of saying he's shedding the legacy promotional services businesses that got bundled in over decades. He's also outsourcing IT and signalling that the mass layoff phase is over. What this tells you is that the world's largest agency network is in active reorganization around AI capability as the core. For a consultant, that's a market signal: the holding companies are contracting their breadth and deepening their AI investment. Independent consultants who can do what the holding companies can't — move fast, advise with specificity, and not bill for a team of twelve when two will do — have a genuine window here.

Meanwhile, Marketing Dive published research this morning on a shift in how consumers are defining success — and it's the kind of brand-strategy insight you'd want in your back pocket. The finding is that Americans still have big aspirations, but they're measuring success through wellbeing, belonging, and purpose rather than status markers. For any brand or institution that has been communicating achievement and prestige — and that includes universities — this is a signal to recalibrate the value proposition. Canadian universities in particular have been selling credentials and rankings. The research suggests the audience increasingly wants to hear about community, transformation, and meaning. That's a strategic reframe that takes consulting expertise to execute.

And there's a useful case study out of Chief Marketer on Everpure's rebrand — a B2B industrial brand that went through a full repositioning for the AI era. The takeaway is that AI-era B2B marketing requires clearer differentiation, faster content iteration, and purpose-led positioning. The old playbook of spec sheets and trade show presence is dead. This is directly applicable to the way you'd advise a Canadian university competing for research partnerships, faculty, and students in a crowded global marketplace.

Now to higher education, and I want to flag three stories that each touch your world in a different way.

Start with TRU, because this one is genuinely exciting. A student project at Thompson Rivers University has built an AI prototype for early wildfire detection. The system uses AI to identify wildfire signatures faster than traditional monitoring, and it's getting national education media coverage. There are two angles here for you. The first is the obvious local one: you live in Sun Peaks, you know exactly how real the wildfire threat is to Interior BC, and a TRU student team building something that could meaningfully help is worth celebrating. The second angle is the consulting one: TRU is developing applied AI credibility. A university that's producing student AI projects with real-world applications is a university that's starting to think about AI as a strategic capability, not just a classroom conversation. That's a door. If you haven't already mapped out your TRU engagement strategy, this is a moment to think about it.

The second story, also out of Kamloops, is a deeper structural issue that Castanet is reporting on today: BC's legacy post-secondary funding formula is under scrutiny for creating systemic inequity between universities. The argument is that older, more established institutions locked in funding advantages decades ago that newer institutions like TRU have never been able to overcome, regardless of enrolment growth or program quality. This is exactly the kind of structural constraint that a smart institutional strategy has to work around rather than through. If you're advising TRU or any other newer Canadian institution, the funding inequity story is the context that explains why marketing and brand-building matter so much — if you can't win on budget, you have to win on positioning.

And then there's France, which is now aggressively marketing itself to international researchers as doctoral enrolments decline globally. France is launching new incentive packages, streamlining researcher visas, and positioning itself as the stable, welcoming alternative to the US in a moment of American immigration chaos. For Canadian universities, this is a competitive pressure they haven't fully felt yet. Canada has benefited enormously from the US becoming less welcoming to international talent. France is now making the same play. Any Canadian institution that thinks it can simply wait for talent to arrive needs to hear this story.

A couple of global items worth your attention this morning.

Axios has a piece that's framed around Jonathan Swan's new book with Maggie Haberman — Regime Change — which is apparently credible enough that it triggered a West Wing leak hunt the moment it started circulating. Swan shared three things that CEOs should specifically understand about how Trump thinks: he operates on a Great Man theory of history and responds to leaders who play to that; he cares about deals as ends in themselves, not just as policy outcomes; and loyalty is a live transaction, not a credential you bank. This isn't partisan framing — it's practical operational intelligence for any executive with US market exposure. Given that your real estate holdings and consulting clients all exist in a North American context shaped by US policy, understanding the operating logic of the current administration is useful.

Also today: the US student loan overhaul takes effect July first, tomorrow. The SAVE plan — which millions of borrowers were depending on — is being eliminated, repayment options are being narrowed, and borrowers have ninety days to pick a new plan or get auto-enrolled in something more expensive. The direct impact is on American borrowers, but the indirect impact is relevant to Canadian institutions. Graduate students who planned around SAVE are now facing materially higher debt burdens, which changes the cost calculation for pursuing advanced degrees in the US. Canadian graduate programs that communicate value clearly and move on recruitment could pick up talented American students who are reconsidering their options. This is a conversation worth having with any Canadian university admissions team you're advising.

Locally, two items from Kamloops this morning.

On the celebratory side: thousands of people packed Riverside Park to watch Canada advance at the FIFA World Cup, and by all accounts it was one of those rare civic moments where a city just exhales together. If you were in Kamloops this weekend, you felt it. Canada beating South Africa and moving through the tournament is producing genuine national joy in a summer that's had plenty of anxiety — good energy heading into Canada Day tomorrow.

And a health alert that's directly relevant to BC families: doctors published a detailed case report this morning on the 2024 Ontario death of a child who contracted rabies from bat contact. The case is being released publicly specifically to renew warnings about bat exposure, and the message is simple and serious: any skin contact with a bat — even something as small as a scratch you might not notice — requires immediate medical attention. With your family spending summer time in Sun Peaks, where bat activity in and around buildings is not uncommon, this is worth knowing. The post-exposure window for effective treatment is narrow, and the consequence of missing it is fatal. Please share this with your family.

And one item in the national safety category that I don't want to bury: a Northwest Territories community was evacuated this weekend due to wildfire. This is the first major NWT evacuation of the 2026 wildfire season, and it's consistent with the pattern of the last several years where the season escalates earlier and burns hotter than forecasters model. For you in Sun Peaks, this is a season-opening reminder. Know your evacuation routes. Know where your important documents are. Know what the alert levels mean in the Sun Peaks and Kamloops area. BC Wildfire Service updates are worth checking every few days through July and August. This isn't catastrophizing — it's the practical reality of where you live and how much you love it.

That's your Monday briefing, Midya — the last Monday of June. The big strategic takeaway this week is that the agentic AI shift in marketing is no longer coming; it's here, and Cannes Lions confirmed it as the new baseline. Your job as a consultant is to be the person who helps clients understand what that actually means for their specific organization — not the abstraction, but the practical implementation. The TRU wildfire AI story and the BC funding equity story together suggest that your most local potential client is doing interesting things and facing structural challenges that a smart strategist could genuinely help with. Start the week with that conversation in mind. Happy Canada Day tomorrow — enjoy it.
